newsitem.title: USA: Colonial Pipeline extends distillate allocations.
newsitem.headline: Colonial Pipeline extends distillate allocations.

text.p: Colonial Pipeline Co, still faced with more shipping demand than its huge Houston-to-New York distillate line can handle, extended space allocations on the line through January 1997, a Colonial official said.
The official also said he "would not be surprised" if Colonial again extended the allocations through February.
"We have more demand than we have capacity," the Colonial official said, noting Colonial advised its clients of the new allocations on Wednesday.
Responding to a question, the official also said: "It's way too early to tell, but the way things have gone this year I would not be surprised to see allocations extended through February as well."
He said shipping demand on its parallel gasoline pipeline has also swelled recently, though Colonial now has no plans to allocate shipping space on that line as well.

The strong demand on the gasoline has precluded the use of the gasoline line to move even more distillates -- mainly heating oil, to the populous Northeast, where heating oil remains the main source of heat for homes.
Colonial had opened its gasoline lines to distillates in late October through November as part of the original allocation announcement.
The move to extend allocations, due to continued overwhelming demand on the line, follows similar pro-rations that began in late October, and were extended through November, then December.

The allocations began amid industry concern, since modulated, that inventories of heating oil were far too low for comfort ahead of winter in the Northeast, the largest heating oil market in the world.
Many industry sources now believe that record refinery heating oil output should be enough to meet most demand.

But sceptics note a real blast of winter cold has yet to test the new cost-conscious hand-to-mouth inventory philosophy that is gripping the U.S. oil industry, and that it is not at all clear the industry could meet sustained weather-driven demand without the cushion of more voluminous inventories.

The arterial Colonial Pipeline extends from Houston to Linden, New Jersey, on the edge of New York Harbor, and can move as much as 960,000 barrels per day (bpd) of distillates and 1.2 million bpd of gasoline.

Atlanta-based Colonial is a consortium of 10 oil companies, including Amoco Corp, Atlantic Richfield Co, Petroleos de Venezuela SA's Citgo Petroleum Co unit, DuPont Co's Conoco Inc, Mobil Corp, Phillips Petroleum Co, Texaco Inc, Union Oil, a Unocal Corp unit, and Marathon Oil Co, a USX-Marathon Group unit.
-- Oliver Ludwig, New York Energy Desk 1 212 859 1633
